title: Delirium vs Dementia: Acute Change Is a Medical Problem
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating change in attention and cognition that should trigger a search for reversible causes such as infection, medication effects, dehydration, hypoxia, pain, constipation, or urinary retention. Do not dismiss sudden confusion as 'just dementia.'
recognize: Abrupt onset, fluctuating attention, altered sleep-wake cycle, disorganized thinking, and change from baseline favor delirium.
Dementia is typically chronic and progressive, but either condition can coexist.
priorities: Compare with baseline and identify acute physiologic or medication triggers.
Escalate sudden mental-status change, especially with instability, focal deficit, hypoxia, fever, or suspected sepsis.
assessMonitor: Cognition/attention, VS, oxygenation, pain, hydration, bowel/bladder, medications, sleep, mobility, and infection cues.
interventions: Promote orientation, hydration, mobility, sleep hygiene, sensory aids, and treatment of causes while minimizing unnecessary restraints/sedatives.
medicationSafety: Anticholinergics, sedatives, opioids, and other CNS-active drugs can precipitate/worsen delirium; medication reconciliation is essential.
teaching: Families should report sudden behavior or attention changes rather than assuming dementia progression.
delegationScope: Routine observation can be delegated; interpretation of acute change and escalation remain licensed-nurse responsibilities.
examTrap: Using a PRN sedative as the first response to new confusion without assessing reversible causes.
oneLinePearl: Sudden confusion is delirium until proven otherwise.
sourceBasis: CMS MDS 3.0 RAI Manual current 2026 resident assessment framework

title: Older Adult Falls: Injury and Cause Both Matter
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: After a fall, first assess for injury and acute deterioration, then investigate why the fall happened. Medication effects, orthostasis, infection, delirium, poor vision, footwear, environmental hazards, and mobility decline are common contributors.
recognize: Head strike, anticoagulant use, new pain, deformity, inability to bear weight, neurologic change, or loss of consciousness increases concern.
priorities: Do not automatically lift the resident before injury assessment.
Escalate head injury, neurologic change, major pain/deformity, bleeding, or instability.
assessMonitor: Neuro status, pain, mobility, skin, VS/orthostasis, medications, vision, footwear, environment, and fall circumstances.
interventions: Use individualized prevention: mobility aids, toileting plan, lighting, footwear, medication review, and strength/balance support.
medicationSafety: Sedatives, antihypertensives, hypoglycemics, opioids, and anticholinergics may increase fall risk.
teaching: Fall prevention works best when matched to the person’s actual risks rather than using restraints.
delegationScope: Post-fall assessment requires licensed nursing judgment; prevention tasks may be shared after plan is established.
examTrap: Putting every high-risk resident on bed rest or restraints to prevent falls.
oneLinePearl: A fall is both an injury event and a symptom with a cause.

title: Older Adult Dehydration: Subtle Changes Count
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Older adults may develop dehydration with less thirst and subtle symptoms. New confusion, orthostasis, dry mouth, constipation, reduced urine, weakness, tachycardia, or functional decline should trigger fluid-status assessment.
recognize: Diuretics, fever, diarrhea, swallowing difficulty, dependence for drinking, and cognitive impairment increase risk.
priorities: Assess intake/output and perfusion in context and identify barriers to drinking.
Escalate hypotension, oliguria, acute kidney injury signs, severe confusion, or inability to take fluids safely.
assessMonitor: Weight trend, intake/output, BP/orthostasis, HR, mucosa, urine, cognition, mobility, and ordered labs.
interventions: Offer preferred fluids frequently when safe, assist with access, coordinate swallowing needs, and follow fluid orders/restrictions.
medicationSafety: Diuretics and renally cleared drugs may need review during dehydration; never stop medications independently.
teaching: Regular fluids may be needed even when thirst is weak.
delegationScope: Offering fluids can be delegated; fluid-status interpretation and escalation require licensed nursing judgment.
examTrap: Assuming poor intake is harmless because the resident is not asking for water.
oneLinePearl: Older adults may be dehydrated before they feel thirsty.

title: Dysphagia and Aspiration: Coughing Is Not the Only Clue
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Wet voice, throat clearing, pocketing, prolonged meals, recurrent pneumonia, weight loss, or oxygen change during meals can signal dysphagia even without dramatic choking. Follow the prescribed texture/liquid plan and escalate new swallowing change.
recognize: Stroke, dementia, Parkinson disease, frailty, and poor dentition increase risk.
Silent aspiration may occur without cough.
priorities: Stop oral intake if swallowing suddenly appears unsafe and escalate.
Use upright positioning and prescribed texture/pace strategies.
assessMonitor: Voice, cough, respiratory status, meal duration, pocketing, intake, weight, hydration, and fever.
interventions: Position upright, use ordered diet consistency, small bites/sips, oral care, and speech-language pathology plan.
medicationSafety: Do not crush medications into food unless the drug/formulation is safe to crush and the swallowing plan permits it.
teaching: Follow the exact swallowing plan rather than improvising thinner liquids or mixed textures.
delegationScope: Feeding may be delegated only with a clear plan and trained caregiver; new swallowing changes require licensed reassessment.
examTrap: Offering thin water to 'wash down' food when thickened liquids are prescribed.
oneLinePearl: Aspiration can be silent—watch voice, breathing, meals, and recurrent chest infections.

title: Pressure Injury Prevention: Mobility, Moisture, Nutrition, Skin
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Pressure injury prevention requires individualized repositioning/off-loading, moisture management, nutrition/hydration support, skin inspection, and device awareness. Do not massage persistent redness over a bony prominence.
recognize: Immobility, poor perfusion, incontinence, malnutrition, friction/shear, and medical devices increase risk.
priorities: Inspect high-risk skin and off-load pressure consistently.
Escalate nonblanching erythema, deep tissue discoloration, blistering, drainage, odor, or systemic infection cues.
assessMonitor: Skin, mobility, moisture, nutrition, device contact points, pain, and wound changes.
interventions: Reposition per individualized plan, use support surfaces/off-loading, barrier care, and nutrition/wound referrals.
medicationSafety: Pain control can improve mobility but sedating medications may worsen immobility/fall risk.
teaching: Skin protection requires movement and moisture control, not just creams.
delegationScope: Repositioning/skin care may be delegated; staging and deterioration assessment require licensed competency per policy.
examTrap: Massaging a reddened bony prominence to improve circulation.
oneLinePearl: Off-load pressure before skin breaks down.

title: Polypharmacy: New Symptom? Review the Medication List
bottomLine: Falls, confusion, constipation, urinary retention, orthostasis, sedation, and appetite changes may be medication effects rather than new diseases. Medication reconciliation should include prescription, OTC, PRN, supplements, timing, and recent changes.
recognize: Multiple prescribers, renal impairment, duplicate classes, anticholinergics, CNS depressants, and complex schedules increase risk.
priorities: Identify recent additions/dose changes and high-risk combinations.
Report adverse-effect patterns and do not independently discontinue chronic medications.
assessMonitor: Mental status, BP/orthostasis, falls, bowel/bladder, sedation, pain, appetite, renal function, and adherence.
interventions: Maintain accurate medication list, simplify administration support when ordered, and communicate suspected adverse effects.
medicationSafety: Avoid assuming 'PRN' means harmless; sedatives, anticholinergics, opioids, hypoglycemics, and anticoagulants warrant particular vigilance.
teaching: Bring all prescription/OTC/supplement products to medication reviews.
delegationScope: Medication reconciliation and adverse-effect assessment require licensed nursing involvement.
examTrap: Adding another medication for a new symptom before considering whether an existing drug caused it.
oneLinePearl: In older adults, every new symptom deserves a medication review.

title: Infection in Older Adults: Fever May Be Absent
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Older adults may present with delirium, weakness, falls, poor intake, tachypnea, functional decline, or hypothermia rather than high fever. New decline should prompt focused infection assessment without reflexively labeling asymptomatic bacteriuria as UTI.
recognize: Respiratory, urinary, skin/wound, and gastrointestinal infections may present atypically.
Chronic bacteriuria is common in long-term care and does not by itself prove symptomatic UTI.
priorities: Assess the whole resident for localizing and systemic signs.
Escalate sepsis physiology, new oxygen need, hypotension, altered mental status, or rapid decline.
assessMonitor: VS, respiratory status, urine symptoms, wounds, hydration, cognition, intake, and function.
interventions: Use infection-control precautions, obtain ordered testing based on symptoms, and support timely antimicrobial treatment when indicated.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary antibiotic use for positive urine tests without compatible clinical findings; follow stewardship/prescriber guidance.
teaching: Report sudden weakness, confusion, breathing change, or poor intake even without a high fever.
delegationScope: Routine observations can be delegated; synthesis of atypical infection cues requires licensed nursing judgment.
examTrap: Diagnosing UTI from cloudy urine or bacteriuria alone.
oneLinePearl: No fever does not mean no infection in frail older adults.

title: Constipation and Fecal Impaction: Overflow Diarrhea Can Mislead
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Constipation in older adults can progress to impaction, urinary retention, delirium, anorexia, and overflow liquid stool. New 'diarrhea' in a chronically constipated resident may be leakage around an impaction.
recognize: Low mobility, low fluid/fiber intake, opioids, anticholinergics, iron, and neurologic disease increase risk.
priorities: Assess bowel pattern, abdominal symptoms, medication causes, intake, and red flags before adding laxatives.
Escalate severe pain, vomiting, distention, bleeding, or suspected obstruction.
assessMonitor: Stool frequency/consistency, abdominal findings, appetite, nausea/vomiting, hydration, and medications.
interventions: Use individualized bowel regimen, mobility, fluids/fiber when appropriate, and ordered rectal/oral therapies.
medicationSafety: Do not give stimulant/osmotic agents reflexively when obstruction is possible.
teaching: Regular bowel habits, fluids, movement, and medication review help prevent impaction.
delegationScope: Routine bowel tracking may be delegated; abdominal deterioration requires licensed assessment.
examTrap: Treating overflow stool with an antidiarrheal without considering impaction.
oneLinePearl: Liquid stool can leak around a solid impaction.

title: Urinary Retention in Older Adults: Look Beyond 'No Urine'
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Urinary retention may present as suprapubic discomfort, frequent small voids, overflow incontinence, restlessness, delirium, or reduced output. Medications, constipation, prostate disease, neurologic conditions, and postoperative status are common causes.
recognize: New overflow leakage does not exclude retention.
Anticholinergics and opioids can worsen retention.
priorities: Assess bladder symptoms, output pattern, medications, constipation, and ordered bladder-scan findings.
Escalate acute painful retention, AKI signs, fever/sepsis, or gross hematuria.
assessMonitor: Voids, bladder distention/pain, urine, bowel pattern, medications, and renal status.
interventions: Use scheduled toileting, mobility, privacy, and catheterization only when ordered/indicated.
medicationSafety: Review anticholinergic burden and other retention-promoting drugs; do not stop abruptly without orders.
teaching: Report weak stream, incomplete emptying, or new overflow leakage.
delegationScope: Routine toileting may be delegated; retention assessment and catheter decisions require licensed/prescriber plan.
examTrap: Assuming frequent small voids mean the bladder is emptying adequately.
oneLinePearl: Overflow can be a sign of a full bladder, not an empty one.

title: Acute Functional Decline: A New Dependence Is a Clinical Cue
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A resident who suddenly needs more help walking, eating, dressing, toileting, or transferring may be showing illness, pain, delirium, medication toxicity, dehydration, infection, or neurologic/cardiopulmonary change. Do not normalize abrupt loss of function as aging.
recognize: Decline can precede classic disease symptoms in frail adults.
priorities: Compare function with established baseline and assess for reversible causes.
Escalate acute focal weakness, dyspnea, chest pain, severe pain, delirium, or rapid decline.
assessMonitor: Mobility, ADLs, cognition, pain, VS, oxygenation, intake, bowel/bladder, medications, and falls.
interventions: Treat identified causes, maintain safe mobility, use therapy/restorative nursing plans, and prevent deconditioning.
medicationSafety: Sedation, hypotension, hypoglycemia, and extrapyramidal effects can present as functional decline.
teaching: Families/staff should report sudden changes in what the resident can do independently.
delegationScope: ADL assistance may be delegated; interpretation of new decline and plan changes require licensed nursing judgment.
examTrap: Documenting 'needs more assistance due to age' without assessing why function changed.
oneLinePearl: Function is a vital sign in frail older adults.
sourceBasis: CMS MDS functional abilities framework updated 2026
